subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Decreasing the significance level from 5% to 1% in a test has the effect of:
options: Having no effect on the critical region
Making it harder to reject H0 (smaller critical region)
Increasing the Type I error probability
Making it easier to reject H0
questions.explain: A smaller significance level shrinks the critical region, so stronger evidence is needed to reject H0 and the Type I error probability falls.

questions.q: For a two-tailed test at the 5% level, the critical region is split as:
questions.explain: A two-tailed 5% test places 2.5% in each tail.

questions.q: A test of H0: p = 0.5 vs H1: p > 0.5 with n = 10 gives observed X = 9. If P(X >= 9) = 0.0107 under H0, at the 5% level you should:
questions.explain: Since p-value 0.0107 < 0.05, the result is significant and H0 is rejected.

questions.q: A normal-mean test gives z = 2.4 for H1: mu > mu0 at the 5% level (critical value 1.645). The conclusion is:
options: A Type II error has occurred
Reject H0; evidence the mean has increased
questions.explain: Since 2.4 > 1.645, z is in the critical region, so H0 is rejected.

questions.q: The p-value of a test is best described as:
options: The probability that H0 is true
The probability of a Type II error
The probability, assuming H0 true, of a result at least as extreme as observed
questions.explain: The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result as extreme or more extreme than observed, given H0 is true.

questions.q: For a binomial test H0: p = 0.2 vs H1: p > 0.2 with n = 20, a one-tailed 5% level, the p-value is computed as:
questions.explain: For an upper-tailed test the p-value is P(X >= observed) using p = 0.2 from H0.

questions.q: A product mean weight is meant to be 500 g. A test concludes 'reject H0', but in fact the mean really is 500 g. This is:
questions.explain: Rejecting a true H0 is a Type I error.

questions.q: A Type I error occurs when you:
options: Fail to reject H0 when H0 is false
Reject H0 when H0 is false
Accept H0 when H0 is actually true
Reject H0 when H0 is actually true
questions.explain: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

questions.q: For a two-tailed test on a normal mean at the 5% level, H0 is rejected if |z| exceeds:
questions.explain: A two-tailed 5% test has critical values +/-1.96.

questions.q: A test where the alternative hypothesis is of the form p != 0.5 is described as:
questions.explain: An alternative using 'not equal to' considers both directions, so the test is two-tailed.

questions.q: A test of H0: p = 0.3 vs H1: p < 0.3 with n = 25 gives observed X = 4. If P(X <= 4) = 0.0905 under H0, at the 5% level you should:
questions.explain: Since 0.0905 > 0.05, the result is not significant, so H0 is not rejected.

questions.q: A sample of n = 16 from N(mu, 36) tests H0: mu = 50. The standard deviation of the sample mean (standard error) is:
questions.explain: Standard error = sqrt(sigma^2/n) = sqrt(36/16) = 6/4 = 1.5.

questions.q: A correlation test gives r = 0.31 with critical value 0.49 at the chosen level. The conclusion is:
options: Correlation is proven to be zero
Fail to reject H0; insufficient evidence of correlation
questions.explain: Since 0.31 < 0.49, r is not extreme enough, so H0 (rho = 0) is not rejected.

questions.q: For a one-tailed test on a normal mean at the 5% level (upper tail), H0 is rejected if the test statistic z exceeds:
questions.explain: The upper 5% critical value of the standard normal is 1.645.

questions.q: For a test on a normal mean with known variance, the sample mean X-bar of n observations from N(mu, sigma^2) has distribution:
questions.explain: The distribution of the sample mean is N(mu, sigma^2/n).

questions.q: Testing H0: mu = 80 vs H1: mu > 80 with sigma = 10, n = 100, sample mean 82. The test statistic z is:
questions.explain: Standard error = 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so z = (82 - 80)/1 = 2.

questions.q: If the p-value is less than the significance level, the correct decision is to:
questions.explain: When p < significance level, the result is significant and H0 is rejected.

questions.q: For a correlation test, H0: rho = 0 against H1: rho > 0 is a test of whether there is:
options: Positive linear association in the population
questions.explain: H1: rho > 0 tests for evidence of positive linear correlation in the population.

questions.q: In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis H0 typically states:
options: The parameter equals a specified value (no change/effect)
questions.explain: H0 is the default assumption that the parameter takes a stated value, representing no change or effect.

questions.q: If a test statistic falls inside the critical region, you should:
options: Reject H0 in favour of H1
questions.explain: A test statistic in the critical region leads to rejecting H0 in favour of H1.

questions.q: The significance level of a test represents:
options: The probability of accepting a false H0
The probability of rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true
questions.explain: The significance level is the probability of rejecting a true H0 (a Type I error).

questions.q: A correlation test uses sample r against a critical value from tables. If |r| exceeds the critical value, you should:
questions.explain: If the sample r is more extreme than the critical value, H0 (rho = 0) is rejected.

questions.q: A correct contextual conclusion after failing to reject H0 in a one-tailed test is:
options: 'A Type I error has been made'
'There is insufficient evidence at this level that the mean has increased'
questions.explain: Failing to reject H0 means there is insufficient evidence to support the alternative, stated tentatively and in context.

questions.q: In a context, rejecting H0: p = 0.1 in favour of H1: p > 0.1 should be interpreted as:
options: There is evidence that the true proportion exceeds 0.1
questions.explain: Rejecting H0 for H1: p > 0.1 means there is evidence the true proportion is greater than 0.1.

questions.q: In a binomial test H0: p = 0.4 vs H1: p < 0.4, a small observed number of successes would give a p-value calculated as:
questions.explain: A lower-tailed alternative uses the lower tail probability P(X <= observed).

questions.q: Failing to reject H0 means:
options: A Type I error has occurred
There is insufficient evidence against H0
questions.explain: Not rejecting H0 indicates insufficient evidence against it, not proof that it is true.

questions.q: Testing H0: mu = 100 vs H1: mu != 100 with sigma^2 = 25, n = 25, sample mean 102. The test statistic z is:
questions.explain: Standard error = sqrt(25/25) = 1, so z = (102 - 100)/1 = 2.

questions.q: A two-tailed normal-mean test gives z = -1.2 at the 5% level (critical values +/-1.96). The conclusion is:
options: The mean is proven equal to mu0
Reject H0 since z is negative
questions.explain: Since |-1.2| < 1.96, the statistic is outside the critical region, so H0 is not rejected.

questions.q: When testing a product-moment correlation coefficient, the population value tested under H0 is usually denoted:
questions.explain: The population correlation coefficient is denoted rho; the sample value r is the test statistic.

questions.q: A coin is tested for bias with H0: p = 0.5 against H1: p > 0.5, where p is the probability of heads. Under H0, the number of heads X in n tosses follows:
questions.explain: Under H0, X ~ B(n, 0.5).
